# Analysis: Turtle Trading System 2 (Donchian Breakout) — REJECT

**Why this outcome is consistent with the mechanism.** System 2 is a pure long-term trend-following breakout: it wins big and rarely (win_rate 26.1%, profit_factor 1.32), relying on a handful of extended trends to pay for many small losses. That pattern shows up clearly in the monthly returns — three months (2023-10 at +43.7%, 2024-02 at +35.6%, 2024-06 at +14.4%) drive nearly all the cumulative gain, sitting inside a long stretch of grinding, choppy negative months (Oct-21 through Jun-22, most of 2025). The rolling-annual series confirms this: performance rockets from -42% to +147% by Feb-2024 on the back of that trend cluster, then decays steadily back to negative territory through most of 2025 as breakouts whipsawed. This is exactly the fragility the auditor flagged: in-sample/walk-forward captured the 2023-24 trend window, but the OOS expectancy of -113.67 shows the strategy did not find comparable trends on unseen data — it needs rare, large, sustained moves that didn't recur.

# Analysis: Cross-Sectional Momentum — REJECT

The in-sample/walk-forward picture looks superficially strong: 224 trades, PF 1.80, Sharpe 0.97, Sortino 2.75, CAGR 23.6%, expectancy +1357.92 per trade. But the auditor's verdict rests on the one number that matters most — **out-of-sample expectancy of -54.02** — meaning the edge the backtest found does not survive on data the model never touched. This is a classic overfitting signature: a momentum ranking system with a 126-day time-stop, no skip period, and single-vintage entries has many degrees of freedom (formation window, ranking universe, sector mix) that can fit in-sample noise without capturing a repeatable cross-sectional effect.

The return concentration corroborates this fragility: monthly returns are dominated by a handful of outsized months (Dec-2023 +70%, Aug-2026 +57%, several +40% months) sitting alongside frequent double-digit negative months (2025 alone gave back -55.6% annually). A strategy with genuine cross-sectional edge shouldn't need a small number of "jackpot" months to carry the whole track record. P&L is also sector-concentrated — Capital Goods (+148k) and Financial Services (+88k) account for the bulk of profit, while Chemicals (-22.6k), Metals & Mining (-16.6k) and Realty (-13.2k) bled steadily — suggesting the model rode a few sector-momentum waves rather than a diversified, structural effect. Regime split (bullish 213k vs bearish 91k) shows it only worked when Nifty was already trending, consistent with momentum being regime-dependent rather than robust.

Follow-up ideas: (1) test the paper's actual overlapping-portfolio (multi-vintage) construction to see if smoothing removes the OOS collapse — single-vintage variance may be masking a real but weaker signal; (2) reintroduce the skip period and re-run OOS specifically on 2025 data, where reversal contamination looks worst.

**Mechanism mismatch drove the outcome.** This backtest measures only the long, unlevered, low-beta stock-selection leg — not the paper's actual claim (a leverage-scaled, beta-neutral long-low-beta/short-high-beta spread). # Analysis: Betting Against Beta — REJECT

The verdict rests on one dominant fact: out-of-sample expectancy is -4.88/trade despite a rosy full-sample expectancy of +175.4 and rolling annual returns that peaked near +49% in mid-2024. This is a textbook in-sample/regime-decay pattern, not noise — the strategy's fortunes track the 2023-2024 bull run almost exactly (rolling annual return climbs from ~6% in Jan-2023 to ~49% by Jul-2024) and then deteriorates sharply from late-2024 onward (rolling annual return falls to -11.8% by Oct-2025), coinciding with sharp monthly drawdowns (Oct-24: -9.3%, Feb-25: -9.2%, Mar-26: -16.1%). The P&L-by-regime split (bullish 64,714 vs bearish 5,270) confirms the edge was never really "low-beta outperformance" in a risk-managed sense — it was a long-only, unlevered equity book that made money because Indian equities rallied, and low-beta names simply rode that rally with less drag. Once the tailwind faded, the walk-forward/OOS window exposed the strategy as having no genuine standalone edge. This is consistent with the disclosed scope gap: without the paper's leverage-scaled, beta-neutral construction, you're only capturing the long low-beta leg, which the paper itself predicts is the smaller, directionally-exposed half of the true factor — exactly the kind of construction that looks fine in a bull sample and fails once beta stops being a good proxy for "safety" in a genuinely new period. Sector data reinforces market-beta dependence rather than idiosyncratic stock-picking skill: gains concentrated in cyclical/consumer-discretionary sectors (Auto 21k, Consumer Services 11.9k, Financial Services 10.6k) that thrive in risk-on tapes, while defensive/rate-sensitive FMCG (-6.4k) and Chemicals (-3.2k) — sectors that should theoretically benefit from a true low-beta premium in a chop/down market — actually lost money. That is the opposite of what a working low-beta anomaly should show in a weak-regime OOS slice.

Follow-ups for a future hypothesis: (1) Test a genuine long-short or at least a long/cash market-neutral overlay (e.g., inverse-index futures proxy) once short/leverage infrastructure exists, to isolate the factor from beta-1 market direction — this result cannot distinguish "low beta works" from "long equities worked in 2023-24." The verdict rests entirely on sample size, not on the shape of the numbers themselves. **Why the verdict makes sense given the mechanism**

The in-sample/overall numbers (expectancy ₹509, profit factor 1.74, Sharpe 0.86) look attractive, but they come from the zero-cost, same-day-close backtest — precisely the number the auditor was told not to trust as the deciding metric. The Amihud illiquidity premium is, by construction, a bet on the least-liquid, top-decile-ILLIQ names. That is exactly the strategy type for which execution-realism adjustments (next-day-open fills, ADV-capped sizing, ILLIQ-derived slippage) bite hardest — the slippage model was calibrated to a median-liquidity stock, and this strategy deliberately trades far less liquid names, so realistic costs should be larger than the calibration anchor implies. Once those costs and next-day fill slippage are applied, the -₹148.31 out-of-sample expectancy indicates the "premium" investors were harvesting in the frictionless backtest is mechanically an illiquidity/transaction-cost artifact, not a durable edge that survives real execution.

**Dependency patterns**
The overall P&L is heavily concentrated: Capital Goods (₹25.8k) and Healthcare (₹15.5k) alone account for most of the gains, while Automobile/Auto Components (-₹10.2k) and several other sectors are net negative — a narrow, sector-concentrated return source, not broad-based confirmation of an illiquidity premium. Returns also depend almost entirely on bullish-regime days (₹59.5k vs ₹4.2k bearish), suggesting the "premium" is really a beta/illiquidity-in-rallies effect that evaporates or reverses once trading frictions and adverse regimes are priced in.

**Follow-ups**
1. Re-test with regime-conditioned entries (bullish-only) and sector caps to see if the OOS expectancy turns positive once concentration risk is controlled.
2. Explore a lower illiquidity threshold (e.g., top-quintile instead of top-decile) to reduce ADV-cap/slippage drag while retaining some illiquidity tilt.

# Analysis: Betting Against Beta — REJECT

**Why the numbers look this way.** The headline in-sample/overall figures (expectancy +110.1, PF 1.21, CAGR 7.13%) look mediocre-but-tolerable, yet the auditor's decisive check — out-of-sample expectancy of -15.19/trade — flips the verdict. This is consistent with the mechanism being tested here: we only capture the long, unlevered low-beta stock-selection leg, not the paper's leverage-scaled, beta-neutral long-short spread. A one-sided, unlevered low-beta book has much weaker structural edge than the documented factor, so it's unsurprising the edge doesn't survive genuinely unseen data even though it looked fine walk-forward. Compounding this, the 1-year (vs. paper's 3–5 year) volatility/correlation lookback makes beta estimates noisier and more regime-reactive, which plausibly degrades stock selection precisely in the out-of-sample window.

**Dependencies.** Returns were almost entirely a 2021 phenomenon (+33.3% in 2021 vs -10.4% in 2022), and concentrated in a bullish regime (+27,650 bullish vs -4,750 bearish) and one sector (Telecommunication +23,166, offsetting Oil Gas & Consumable Fuels -10,538 and Consumer Durables -3,457). A long-only low-beta anomaly leaning this hard on a single bull-market year and one sector is fragile, not diversified — exactly the profile that fails to replicate out-of-sample.

**Follow-ups.** (1) Test whether the edge is really sector-driven (ex-Telecom) rather than a genuine beta effect. (2) Once short/leverage infrastructure exists, re-test the true beta-neutral long-short spread rather than the long-only proxy, which this result cannot speak to.

# Performance Analysis: Betting Against Beta (Low-Beta Anomaly) — REJECT

**Why the verdict stands despite decent aggregate numbers:** The full-sample metrics (Sharpe 0.91, expectancy +129.42, PF 1.30) look respectable, but these are dominated by in-sample/walk-forward periods. The auditor's -8.90 out-of-sample expectancy is the disqualifying number, and the monthly return pattern explains why: strong, broad-based gains cluster in 2024 (annual +30.2%), then the edge deteriorates sharply — 2025 is essentially flat (+0.03%) with five losing months including two >6% drawdowns (Oct -6.6%, Feb -7.5%), and 2026 opens with a -12.96% March before a partial April/May recovery. This is a classic in-sample-good/out-of-sample-fails pattern, exactly what the auditor flagged.

**Mechanism and dependencies:** This backtest only captures the long, unlevered low-beta stock-selection leg — not the paper's levered, beta-neutral long-short spread — so it was structurally never going to reproduce the paper's documented magnitude, only a diluted, one-sided fraction of it. Returns are almost entirely regime-dependent: bullish-day entries generated $34,024 of the $34,944 total P&L (97%), with bearish-day entries contributing almost nothing ($920). This is not a beta-hedged, market-neutral return stream — it's a long-only equity strategy that happens to work when Nifty is rising and stalls or loses money otherwise, consistent with 2025's choppier, more range-bound tape versus 2024's stronger uptrend. Sector concentration reinforces this fragility: Healthcare (+$13,240) and Automobiles (+$12,588) alone account for more than the entire net P&L, while Financial Services (-$7,444), Chemicals (-$2,455), and Services (-$2,249) bled steadily — a narrow, sector-idiosyncratic engine rather than a diversified factor premium.

**Follow-ups:** (1) Test true beta-neutral construction (long low-beta / short high-beta, if/when SLB infra exists) to see if the paper's actual claim — not this diluted proxy — holds out-of-sample. (2) Investigate whether the 1-year vol/correlation lookback (vs. paper's 5-year) is injecting noise that causes late-sample beta misclassification, given the OOS breakdown coincides with the shortened-window regime.

# Analysis: Cross-Sectional Momentum — REJECT

**Why the verdict follows from the mechanism:** With only 69 trades across a single walk-forward window, the strategy never got the chance to demonstrate repeatability — the auditor's 0/1 positive-expectancy windows finding isn't about the sign of the number so much as the complete absence of a second data point to confirm it wasn't luck. This is compounded by the single-vintage holding construction: instead of the paper's overlapping-portfolio smoothing, each qualifying episode realizes one entry point's path. That mechanically inflates variance — visible in the 19.48% max drawdown against a mere 4.17% return on capital (recovery factor 0.205) and a Sharpe of 0.185 despite a "positive" expectancy of 60.38. The win rate of 30.4% with PF 1.11 shows this is a classic momentum shape (few big winners, many small losers) — but with only one window, we can't tell if the big winners are structural or survivorship of a lucky stretch (the 2026-08 monthly return of +19.72% single-handedly rescues an otherwise negative multi-year P&L, per the -5.38%/-8.32%/+17.87% annual sequence).

**Dependencies:** The strategy leaned entirely on bearish-regime entries (+$8,719) while bleeding in bullish regimes (-$4,553) — the opposite of what a long-only momentum book "should" want, suggesting mean-reversion or short-covering bounces drove entries rather than genuine trend continuation. Sector P&L is concentrated and lopsided: Healthcare/Chemicals/Power carried the book (+$14,374 combined) while Financial Services and IT alone erased over $6,500 — no diversified cross-sectional edge, just a few sector bets.

**Follow-ups:** (1) Extend the walk-forward to multiple J=6/K=6 windows before any re-test — one window is statistically meaningless regardless of the sign. (2) Test whether the bearish-regime dependency is a Nifty-beta artifact rather than idiosyncratic momentum, by conditioning entries on regime explicitly.

# Analysis: MAX Effect (Lottery-Demand Anomaly) — REJECT

**Why the verdict follows from the numbers:** With only a single walk-forward window (0/1 positive), there's no basis to distinguish a genuine lottery-demand premium from noise. The aggregate stats confirm the fragility: a profit factor of 1.02 is essentially breakeven, Sharpe of 0.097 and Sortino of 0.119 are near-zero risk-adjusted signal, and recovery factor of 0.069 shows the strategy barely earns back its 12.85% drawdown. The 38.9% win rate combined with positive expectancy (₹10.13/trade) implies the edge — if real — lives entirely in tail trades, which is precisely the pattern that makes single-window validation untrustworthy (same failure mode as SEED-ORB-2).

**Regime/sector dependency:** The strategy's entire P&L (+₹12,881 bearish vs. -₹11,970 bullish) came from bearish-Nifty-day entries — for a long-only lottery-demand strategy, this is backwards from the retail-chasing mechanism the MAX effect is supposed to capture (overpaying for upside skew typically clusters in bullish/euphoric tape). This inversion suggests the "edge" is regime-contamination, not the anomaly itself. Sector P&L is equally lopsided: Capital Goods, FMCG, and Financial Services carried the book while Construction Materials (-₹5,681) and Consumer Services (-₹3,937) alone erased most gains — concentration risk, not a broad-based factor.

**Follow-up ideas:** (1) Re-run with overlapping-portfolio construction (the paper's actual design) before fully discarding — single-vintage holding is a MODERATE/MATERIAL disclosed deviation that could be masking a real signal. (2) If revisited, condition explicitly on Nifty regime and exclude Construction/Consumer Services/Realty to test whether a cleaner subset shows multi-window consistency.
